questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish a maturity assessment from the KPI dashboards covered in Chapter 3?
options: A dashboard tracks ongoing operational health month to month; a maturity assessment asks a slower-moving question about structural capability over time
They are exactly the same thing with different names
A maturity assessment replaces the need for any KPIs at all
Dashboards are only used once, at program launch
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames the dashboard as the operational view and the maturity assessment as the slower, structural-capability view.

questions.q: Does this lesson claim one official, universally agreed data governance maturity model?
options: Yes — it names one specific vendor's model as the only correct one
The lesson avoids giving any maturity scale at all
Yes — it claims the five levels are a legally mandated standard
No — it explicitly says there is no single official model it claims as authoritative, and describes a generic five-level shape instead
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that different vendors publish their own branded models and that it is teaching the general shape, not a specific proprietary framework.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend scoring dimensions separately rather than giving the whole program one blended score?
options: Blended scores are always more accurate than dimension-level scores
A program is rarely at the same level everywhere, and a blended score would hide specific, actionable gaps like being managed on measurement but ad hoc on adoption
Regulations require every dimension to be scored identically
Scoring dimensions separately is purely a cosmetic preference with no practical benefit
questions.explain: The lesson's own example — managed on measurement, ad hoc on adoption — shows why a single number would obscure the real, actionable gap.

questions.q: Which of these is listed in this lesson as one of the five dimensions to score independently?
options: Marketing budget
Office location
Stewardship
Stock price
questions.explain: The five dimensions named are stewardship, policy and process, measurement, adoption and culture, and tooling.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what should happen with a maturity assessment's results?
options: The results should be filed away and never referenced again
Results should only ever be shared with the program's original champion
The assessment should be repeated immediately with no time allowed to act on it
A weak dimension should become a scoped roadmap item, and an improved dimension should become evidence in the value realization report
questions.explain: The lesson ties the assessment directly back into Lesson 21's roadmap and Lesson 22's funding conversation — an assessment that changes nothing is just an exercise.
